zulip-msg-1737314.trecho: Welcome to today's community event around navigating the code review process!

zulip-msg-1737318.trecho: The general setup with these community events is that folks should start topics in the stream that we're using to ask questions/bring up things that are on your mind or you want to discuss.

zulip-msg-1737319.trecho: The main purpose of the event is just to lower the activation energy / effort required to talk about something -- probably every conversation that we'll have today is one that we could in theory have had any other time asynchronously.

zulip-msg-1737320.trecho: We're here to help answer questions and brainstorm with you about how to make code review in Zulip better.

zulip-msg-1737321.trecho: I'll start a few discussion topics just go get folks talking and provide some examples.

zulip-msg-1737329.trecho: One important line of thought that @_**Tim Abbott** has taught me is to write your PR to make it easy to review your changes.

zulip-msg-1737334.trecho: Can you share some of your own process that way, Aman?

zulip-msg-1737337.trecho: Yeah, like if you are doing a complex change, how would you break it into verifiable small steps which can be their own independent commit.

zulip-msg-1737339.trecho: Do you find yourself editing or re-crafting your commits as you get deeper into a project?

zulip-msg-1737340.trecho: This makes my own life easier too since any further modifications are easier to track and the amount of logic I have to verify after a change gets reduced too.

zulip-msg-1737341.trecho: Yeah I think that's a great point.

zulip-msg-1737349.trecho: I'm also a big fan of `git add -p`, where you can stage just certain parts of your changes to build a commit.

zulip-msg-1737365.trecho: Yeah I really like how it breaks the edited stuff into concise chunks, it made me more productive.

zulip-msg-1737368.trecho: Both tools are useful :) I usually reach for `git stash` when I realize I've gotten WAY ahead of myself, or have something else I realize needs to be completed first. `git add -p` is more for when I either get a little too enthusiastic changing things at once, or when I'm pretty clear the changes I need to put up, and just want to craft commits as I go.

zulip-msg-1737393.trecho: For breaking commits up, one trick I use is to notice when I find myself reaching for the word "Also" when writing a commit message.

zulip-msg-1737394.trecho: You can just select the changes you want to stage and the press the keyboard shortcut to stage it.

zulip-msg-1737397.trecho: I find it really also helps to force every non-trivial commit to really have a *why* to it.

zulip-msg-1737333.trecho: Let's use this topic to talk about challenges with rebasing work.

zulip-msg-1737348.trecho: I want to ask folks their experience regarding this, and what else could we do to make the reordering easier.

zulip-msg-1737350.trecho: Do you folks use the `diff3` conflict mode?

zulip-msg-1737351.trecho: No, I haven't used it until now.

zulip-msg-1737352.trecho: I think the key to being successful with Git is mastering the art of quickly resolving conflicts.

zulip-msg-1737353.trecho: For resolving merge conflicts, I highly recommend using the `diff3` conflict style -- I have it in my global `~/.gitconfig`.

zulip-msg-1737356.trecho: It's not at all a bad idea to practice resolving conflicts, either.

zulip-msg-1737361.trecho: BTW https://github.com/zulip/zulip-gci/blob/master/tasks/2017/git-comfortable.md is an old resource that we made for Google Code-In that might be of some help for folks looking to get more comfortable with Git.

zulip-msg-1737364.trecho: I never quite used the `rebase` command before I started contributing to zulip.Took me a while but now more comfortable.

zulip-msg-1737369.trecho: Now I use it across all other projects.

zulip-msg-1737370.trecho: Yes makes every thing much more efficient and organised.

zulip-msg-1737371.trecho: What the `diff3` mode does is it presents all the information that you need in order to resolve most merge conflicts inline in the file:

zulip-msg-1737375.trecho: Without the `diff3` mode, Git doesn't include all 3 of those blocks, and from a mathematical/logical standpoint, it's often impossible to correctly resolve merge conflicts without using `git log -p <path>` to read the changes that happened in `main` and `git show` to read the commit you're trying to apply and make sense of it all.

zulip-msg-1737377.trecho: Most modern editors have merge-conflict resolution modes that can help use highlighting or whatnot to make the information stand out; it's worth playing with those if you haven't already.

zulip-msg-1737378.trecho: Sometimes the root cause of a merge conflict can be very subtle, on the level of correcting a spelling mistake.

zulip-msg-1737383.trecho: It's also important to run tests / manually retest even after a seemingly trivial merge conflict resolution.

zulip-msg-1737387.trecho: I find something probably like 5-10% of the time, even with all my experience.

zulip-msg-1737392.trecho: Couple that diffing work with the reviewer mindset Tim mentioned, and you'll really get good at catching things that would otherwise slip through.

zulip-msg-1737400.trecho: So if you are able to consistently produce work of that form, it's a huge boon to your overall productivity as a developer, both when working on Zulip and for the rest of your career.

zulip-msg-1737413.trecho: This [message](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/stream/44-git-help/topic/git.20rebase.20to.20make.20branch.20up.20to.20date.20with.20main/near/1517650) from @_**Lauryn Menard**  has been very helpful to me regarding rebasing.

zulip-msg-1737415.trecho: Yeah, it would probably be a good idea to incorporate that into our documentation a bit more.

zulip-msg-1737322.trecho: Let's use this topic to talk about the CI/test failures part of code review!

zulip-msg-1737323.trecho: Feel free to post questions on topic here; I'll also just write a couple paragraphs of reminders.

zulip-msg-1737324.trecho: Probably the most important reminder is that maintainers are much more likely to promptly review work that is passing CI, because a lot of draft/unfinished work doesn't pass the tests, and with limited time, one generally wants to prioritize reviewing work that, at a glance, looks ready for review.

zulip-msg-1737327.trecho: So, one kind of test failure that often troubles me is those which involve making a stub of something, in node tests to get the coverage.

zulip-msg-1737332.trecho: I expect you understand what stubbing actually does but struggle with the syntax to use?

zulip-msg-1737335.trecho: I mean, I have never used stubbing till now... so yeah it is something new to me... but what I understand is you try to create the components to test those parts?

zulip-msg-1737336.trecho: The node tests are fairly finicky, and I think we need to do some architectural work to make them easier to write.

zulip-msg-1737372.trecho: We usually do so to make the behaviour of this external method deterministic.

zulip-msg-1737374.trecho: As for syntax, you are doing it right to look at examples of how other tests use them since we have own methods to create stubs.

zulip-msg-1737376.trecho: and sometimes when I use like `$().find()`, towards the tests side, it expects me to use`set_find_results()`, so like does it involve first stubbing the the main component, and then its child components to write a good test ?

zulip-msg-1737379.trecho: You need to take a step back and first think about what parts of the code you really want to test.

zulip-msg-1737391.trecho: At a high level, the goal of tests is to prevent bugs.

zulip-msg-1737396.trecho: That doesn't mean that one has to write a test for new code you add to that module!

zulip-msg-1737841.trecho: - Is it clear which tests fail? (going into actions, then jobs inside them, knowing the connection to local tests)

zulip-msg-1737843.trecho: In zulip-terminal (ZT), that mostly-sequential behavior is also present in local linting, but in CI the linting parts are split into their own jobs, on a single platform/python.

zulip-msg-1738649.trecho: I think lint running in its own job in CI would be nice; part of the challenge is that `mypy` checks can fail on only some but not all Python versions.

zulip-msg-1738653.trecho: Another part is that our setup steps are absurdly slow (> 5 minutes), and thus expensive to duplicate for the sake of parallelization.

zulip-msg-1738661.trecho: Seeing all the failures is useful for reducing the number of round-trips to fix everything.

zulip-msg-1738668.trecho: I’m not sure if that was a deliberate choice or just the easiest thing to implement.

zulip-msg-1738669.trecho: I'm very aware that other folks are more knowledgeable of the interdependence of elements in that repo :)

zulip-msg-1738670.trecho: Right, that's the point I was referring to with repushing.

zulip-msg-1738672.trecho: I don't think this was discussed; it was likely just not supported in the previous CI system that we ported from.

zulip-msg-1738674.trecho: Though there are trade-offs; having the job be marked as failed and completed is clearer feedback than having to wait for another 8 minutes of tests before the "status" section of the PR shows a failure, and I'm like 75% confident that would be a possible outcome of changing this.

zulip-msg-1738675.trecho: I think the status section will show the failure early if we do it correctly (using the GitHub Actions language to properly express the dependencies between steps, rather than building some janky wrapper script).

zulip-msg-1738677.trecho: But my vague sense is that the biggest change over the last 2-3 years that has made it a lot slower is `test-backend` and `mypy` getting slower as we add more code, and `test-backend` in particular likely has accumulated some number of wasteful tests (as things do).

zulip-msg-1738701.trecho: I agree that there's something to be said for running all jobs every time - or having the option to do so at least.

zulip-msg-1738705.trecho: Could one container be rebuilt much more frequently, to keep setup super-minimal?

zulip-msg-1737326.trecho: Does anyone have feedback on how we could make it better?

zulip-msg-1737395.trecho: Until now, the review checklist has really helped me.

zulip-msg-1737398.trecho: Once my coverage had failed, but I realized it only when the github CI ran.

zulip-msg-1737401.trecho: By coverage, do you mean running the tests locally?

zulip-msg-1737402.trecho: We don't include `--coverage` in the default options for local testing because it makes tests at least 2x slower.

zulip-msg-1737404.trecho: I should mention BTW that I hope everyone is taking full advantage of the features of our testing tools; the `--rerun` options to only rerun the tests the failed, and the fact that all of them support passing a specific test file (or other collections) in order to verify what you'd like to check.

zulip-msg-1737405.trecho: There is a cool trick with `--coverage` that I really like -- if you write a new test, you can run `test-backend --coverage <test_name>` and look at the coverage report it generated to see exactly what code your new test executed.

zulip-msg-1737406.trecho: If testing coverage was mentioned in the review checklist, it would help one remember to check the coverage locally before marking a PR ready for review.

zulip-msg-1737407.trecho: But you can also use it to just quickly check whether the test that you wrote in fact executed the 3 lines that you were hoping to add coverage to.

zulip-msg-1737410.trecho: Yes, that is what I wanted to say exactly :happy:

zulip-msg-1737411.trecho: The node tests are fast enough that checking `--coverage` locally is a good idea; I wouldn't recommend by default running the backend tests with `--coverage` before submitting a PR unless you'll be using the time while it's running to do something else, since it can take several minutes to run, about as long as CI.

zulip-msg-1737414.trecho: I'll often run tests in the background while writing up longer-form commit message explanations or a PR description.

zulip-msg-1737416.trecho: for me, with my 8gb ram, if i run tests coverage locally and do other task simultaneously, then often the tests get stuck and won't execute further.

zulip-msg-1737418.trecho: Often happens that I have to restart my code editor.

zulip-msg-1737419.trecho: We can also put a small review checklist on the issue templates too, could be helpful for people reporting issues for the first time.

zulip-msg-1737425.trecho: Hmm, what do you have in mind for the issue template specifically?

zulip-msg-1737426.trecho: We try to keep the issue templates lightweight to make it not feel like a burden for end users to report bugs -- it's really valuable when folks do report something broken, and I know some projects have issue templates that feel like they take 10 minutes to fill out, which really reduces how much people report stuff.

zulip-msg-1737433.trecho: If the issue template has too much checklist to go through even I may end up confused if this checks out as a bug and end up not reporting it.

zulip-msg-870799.trecho: One thing worth highlighting is that it isn't always intuitive for others what is time-consuming for me when doing code reviews.

zulip-msg-870805.trecho: The reason that a lot of my feedback for new contributors is about commit structure/messages, comments, etc., is that a huge portion of the work for me is understanding a change so that I can model its impact on the product.

zulip-msg-870808.trecho: So those PRs that communicate their changes really clearly and explain how the developer tested to ensure that natural concerns about how it might fail aren't a problem can take 5-10x less time to review than others.

zulip-msg-870811.trecho: So it's not uncommon for me, when in triage mode, to bounce a PR to look at later if it doesn't appear well-explained or I notice something time-consuming I want to do as part of merging it (E.g. rewriting some strings or documentation thoughtfully for posterity).

zulip-msg-589448.trecho: For the next hour or so, I'm here to answer questions people might have for me about Zulip or programming in general.

zulip-msg-589449.trecho: For those of you who don't know me, I'm one of the original ten contributors to Zulip and have a couple thousand commits in the codebase.

zulip-msg-589457.trecho: How did you get involved with Zulip?

zulip-msg-589459.trecho: I was hired by Zulip in 2013.

zulip-msg-589461.trecho: It was a Python project that used wxPython.

zulip-msg-589462.trecho: What were some of the biggest challenges you all faced(if any) during the early days of Zulip?

zulip-msg-589463.trecho: Funding is always a big challenge, although that didn't affect me directly.

zulip-msg-589464.trecho: From a coding perspective, by the time I got there we weren't necessarily solving really hard technical problems; it was more that we wanted to quickly create features that we could test out on our customers.

zulip-msg-589465.trecho: It can be tough to move quickly while maintaining a high quality level.

zulip-msg-589466.trecho: Why VI(M) over other, more modern text editors? :)

zulip-msg-589467.trecho: (just FTR, I'm starting to use VIM more myself; I'm just curious about your opinion)

zulip-msg-589468.trecho: So first of all, there are lots of awesome text editors.

zulip-msg-589469.trecho: I didn't use vim for the first ~15 years that I programmed, even though vi has been around forever, and vim as we know it now has been around for a long time now.

zulip-msg-589470.trecho: Text editors are actually some of the best pieces of software ever written.

zulip-msg-589471.trecho: I used emacs happily for two or three years.

zulip-msg-589472.trecho: I like vim because once you get over the learning curve, which is substantial but definitely feasible, it's minimalism is great for saving keystrokes, and it's available everywhere.

zulip-msg-589473.trecho: The last editor I used other than  vim on a daily basis was Sublime, which was fine, but I missed a few key features from vim, and vim was a bit faster for me.

zulip-msg-589475.trecho: My favorite features in vim are *, #, and control-n/control-p.

zulip-msg-589482.trecho: If you could magically build a software project with ample resources ( within reason ), what would it be?

zulip-msg-589485.trecho: What is your favorite programming language?

zulip-msg-589486.trecho: @**Armaan Ahluwalia** I'd want to build a better browser.

zulip-msg-589487.trecho: Or to rephrase, what would you like to be seen built that maybe currently isn't quite happening?

zulip-msg-589488.trecho: Could you go into more detail? wasm?

zulip-msg-589490.trecho: Let me come back to that question, @**Armaan Ahluwalia**.

zulip-msg-589492.trecho: @**Vishnu Ks** I like Python for getting things done easily.

zulip-msg-589493.trecho: The web stack evolved out of a great system for sharing documents, but all the app stuff is kind of bolted on.

zulip-msg-589494.trecho: I also think there are certain things like CSS that were clearly mistakes on many levels that are just so entrenched now people don't even realize how simple things can be in a well-designed system.

zulip-msg-589497.trecho: The classic example is how hard it is to center a square on a browser page, let 12-year-olds like me could do in TI Basic on computers with less than 1Mb in memory.

zulip-msg-589500.trecho: I also hope that Zulip will some day be a bit more like a browser.

zulip-msg-589503.trecho: Could you paint a picture of what your ideal replacement for CSS would be.

zulip-msg-589504.trecho: The problems with CSS are kind of deep and related to the whole web paradigm that you start an application by laying it out with markup language, when markup language has this strict hierarchy and very limited vocabulary.

zulip-msg-589505.trecho: Then you put lipstick on the pig by having this external stylesheet to add some chrome to the webpage, but the stylesheet isn't really that external since it's deeply coupled to your HTML layout.

zulip-msg-589506.trecho: I think some of the incremental steps people are taking are fine but don't really get at the heart of the problem.

zulip-msg-589507.trecho: I figured your number one gripe would be positioning and layout.

zulip-msg-589508.trecho: At some point you can't have progress making a faster horse, so some time in our lifetime a platform's gonna emerge that tries to knock down 90s-based browsers and there's gonna be some initial pain.

zulip-msg-589509.trecho: Yeah, for stuff like color palettes and fonts, CSS is merely mediocre.

zulip-msg-589510.trecho: Do you think the pace of the web development eco-system helps or hurts developers?

zulip-msg-589511.trecho: As for web assembly, I view that as mostly neutral.

zulip-msg-589512.trecho: I have a degree in CS, but I'm largely self-taught because technology moves so fast and I've generally been curious and wanting to learn new things.

zulip-msg-589513.trecho: But, yeah, there's obviously a concern that if everybody is always chasing the next new thing, you can lose sight of history.

zulip-msg-589514.trecho: Can you shed some light on this if you can?

zulip-msg-589515.trecho: A great example in recent history is that React became really popular in 2015, but the ideas behind it are just making programming more like programming was on early Windows systems, where the constraints of the system created a certain simplicity that actually makes sense.

zulip-msg-589516.trecho: I can only give the short answer for whey Dropbox acquired Zulip.

zulip-msg-589517.trecho: What do you think about free software?

zulip-msg-589519.trecho: Where do you see it going in the future?

zulip-msg-589520.trecho: I think free software is a good thing.

zulip-msg-589522.trecho: Even though git ultimately serves projects that have a strong centralization aspect (including, of course, the inventor of git, who is a strong leader of a project with enormous central control despite the fact that it's license is so open).

zulip-msg-589523.trecho: well, strong leader of several projects, but I mean linux in the above example (and git only in the "meta" sense, haha)

zulip-msg-589524.trecho: Both of the prior questions touch on economic and political realities.

zulip-msg-589525.trecho: What is your advice to software developers who are currently in their early twenties?

zulip-msg-589527.trecho: And the most useful :) Lets hear it!

zulip-msg-589528.trecho: If I went back 25 years ago, I'd be talking to my 23-year old self, and the fact that I was working on C++ at the time was probably pretty reasonable.

zulip-msg-589529.trecho: All my peers were right on top of the web before the older people "got" it, so I think 20-somethings are probably good at seeing trends.

zulip-msg-589530.trecho: I mean, we didn't know you'd be buying airplane tickets on the web (which probably seems ridiculously obvious to any millennial), but we knew the platform was super powerful.

zulip-msg-589531.trecho: If you could obtain one piece of knowledge from any person dead or alive, what would it be?

zulip-msg-589532.trecho: I think my positive advice is that if you're generally curious, you'll get pretty far in life by just keeping up with technologies and try to always be learning, and if machines keep getting faster and global knowledge builds through the internet, you'll be able to build better and better things.

zulip-msg-589533.trecho: Probably my only regret is that you do tend to be short-sighted and too driven by the career markets.

zulip-msg-589534.trecho: Maybe my concrete advice to young 20-somethings is that you want to spend the next five years trying to cast a wide web learning stuff, but try to have a project by the time you're 30 where you've got a five year plan and don't mind a bit of risk because you really want to build it.

zulip-msg-589536.trecho: I don't have a great answer for that.

zulip-msg-589537.trecho: Do you believe there are silos of information that would be useful to make public?

zulip-msg-589539.trecho: So open-source medical AI could be a promising thing.

zulip-msg-589540.trecho: I'm not an expert on medicine, so it's hard for me to speculate on where the advances are gonna come.

zulip-msg-589541.trecho: Interesting that software is now financing medicine too :)

zulip-msg-589544.trecho: Do you have any thoughts on fully remote companies vs traditional companies?

zulip-msg-589545.trecho: I don't think fully remote companies are necessarily more effective than traditional companies, but I like working on a project with people all around the world, and I think the only thing you sacrifice is a bit of "speed of development."  Of course, if you take the long view that we have the next 1000 years to build better software, what's the rush?

zulip-msg-589546.trecho: This is sort of relates back to the earlier questions, where everything about the web's success is success on a 15-year timescale, but it's not necessarily building with the long view in mind.

zulip-msg-589521.trecho: I think there's always a tension between centralization and decentralization.

zulip-msg-589548.trecho: You can put 500 people, mostly American, in a building in San Francisco and build Twitter.

zulip-msg-589549.trecho: Considering you have worked for 4 years (more?) on zulip, what in your mind is the next BIG communication thing.

zulip-msg-870569.trecho: A big part of what underlies that is the huge investment Zulip did in 2015-2017, as the open source project was getting started, in making Zulip accessible to contributors, and specifically with the goal of making it easy for me (after the October 2015 open sourcing, I was the only really active contributor) to review and integrate contributions.

zulip-msg-870571.trecho: For my first 6 months, while I was just doing Zulip nights and weekends at Dropbox, basically all of my personal changes were installer fixes, linter changes, etc., beyond fixing up people's PRs to integrate them.

zulip-msg-870586.trecho: Because of those efforts in tooling, documentation, testing, community processes, etc., it became possible for us to mentor relatively inexperienced folks in a way that makes good use of maintainer time.

zulip-msg-870592.trecho: A lot of open source projects aren't able to get to the point where it takes less time for the maintainers to work with a GSoC student than to just do all the work themselves, and for that reason, they aren't able to run a larger GSoC program unless they're a huge community (like Linux, perhaps).

zulip-msg-870593.trecho: I really notice when I try new OSS projects, how tuned in they are to contributors, though it's different if they're new, use PyPI, old projects, etc.

zulip-msg-870599.trecho: Yeah, one advantage we have is that Zulip has a lot of surface area, so if one's thoughtful, one can point contributors towards places where the polish level isn't so high that it's hard to make progress.

zulip-msg-1420588.trecho: I know it is common for active FOSS projects to have lots of open issues and PRs, but at least, is the PR review blockage not a solvable problem?

zulip-msg-1420642.trecho: This is a complicated topic; I'm about to head to bed so won't write a full essay on it.

zulip-msg-1420643.trecho: The fact is that a large majority of currently open PRs are ~50% complete efforts towards implementing something useful for the project.

zulip-msg-1421106.trecho: With separate repos, the scope of each repo are explicit, and so the expertise needed to maintain the said repo is more localized.

zulip-msg-1421244.trecho: In practice, splitting a project into multiple repositories usually just making changes that cross repository boundaries more complex to manage logistically.

zulip-msg-1421245.trecho: Right now, in practice, we have various other folks who maintain particular parts of the project and do most of the review work for changes to them;

zulip-msg-1421246.trecho: Now, if you are an enormous company like Google and trying to make 10,000s of employees able to work together, there can be good reasons to consider multiple repositories, whether for performance reasons or to allow different divisions within the company to work differently from each other.

zulip-msg-1421248.trecho: Generally the reason we do multiple repositories is for things that we want to be able to version independently from the server/webapp project.

zulip-msg-163341.trecho: The idea is to make it relatively easy for folks to step up as the maintainer for a portion of Zulip, without having to "watch" the entire repository and thus filter through every single issue or PR in the project

zulip-msg-163343.trecho: If you're interested in using this, just ask to join the team and someone will approve

zulip-msg-1748118.trecho: I once accidentally used `git stash pop` twice in a row, which caused some trouble and led to fixing merge conflicts.

zulip-msg-1748638.trecho: Committing instead of stashing may well help with that, because it means you're a bit more hands-on in controlling where the saved changes live and how and when they get re-applied.

zulip-msg-1748639.trecho: But `git stash pop` itself also takes some care to help you deal with that situation.

zulip-msg-1748640.trecho: Note the last line in particular — though it's a little subtle and easy to miss amidst all the other output:

zulip-msg-1748641.trecho: What that means is that because applying the stashed changes hit a merge conflict, the `pop` didn't actually pop — it fell back to doing the equivalent of `git stash apply`.

zulip-msg-1748642.trecho: And therefore if you didn't actually want to apply those changes, you can clear them away with something like `git reset --hard`, and the `git stash pop` will have done no harm.
